sources.citation: Lynch, John, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley. 2002. The Oceanic Languages. Richmond: Curzon.
sources.note: Mondropolon appears only in the listing of Oceanic languages by subgroup (Mid West Manus linkage, p.879). The only stress remark is the family-wide typological generalization (p.35/§3.1: 'Stress is generally fully predictable, falling on the penultimate syllable of a word') which is not specific to Mondropolon.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2021. Counting in the Admiralty Islands. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 39: 19-55. (Glottolog ref 586201.)
sources.note: Mondropolon numerals and tens (lunah '20', co-lunuh '80', tunuh '30', co-cunuh '70', subtractive co-) without stress marks; no prosodic remark.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2021. Eight Languages of the Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia, Special Issue 2021. Front matter / Table of contents / Introduction (18 pp.).
sources.note: Nothing for Mondropolon. Table 0.1 (p.13) lists Mondropolon as language 23 of Blust's 1975 survey with only 4 contact hours over 2 days; it is not among the eight languages sketched (Seimat, Bipi, Lindrou, Sori, Likum, Loniu, Pak, Nauna). Only stress mentions in the file are TOC entries for the Lindrou sketch (Table 3.2, 3.10).

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2021. Eight Languages of the Admiralty Islands. Sketch 2: Bipi; Sketch 5: Likum. LLM Special Issue 2021.
sources.note: Phonology sections are for Likum/Bipi only; Mondropolon is mentioned solely as sharing the coda *t > -k change (Bipi sketch p.158) and the majority numeral pattern (Likum sketch). No Mondropolon stress statement.

sources.note: Nothing: 10 scanned pages (no text) of the handwritten SIL Survey Word List (1999 revision, 120 adaptation, 'Edited for Dunantina Survey, Feb 2017'), items 1-170 (body parts, nature, verbs, adjectives, pronouns, interrogatives). Transcriptions are segmental only (e.g. 76 mondra?an 'big', 78 masi?in 'good', 81 tsu?on 'short', 162 ju 'I', 170 roso 'they'); no stress or length diacritics and no prosodic notes; marginalia concern elicitation ('teeth missing, some t/ts hard to distinguish', 'check - recording wrong'). Read by eye from page renders (pp.1,3,5,10 fully; handwriting, no scanned).

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian Languages (revised ed.). Asia-Pacific Linguistics Open Access Monographs A-PL 008. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Mondropolon indexed at pp. xxxiii, 101 (one of the smallest AN languages), 231 (has contrastive medial geminates), 636 (palatal glide epenthesis before *a). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1996. The linguistic position of the Western Islands, Papua New Guinea. In John Lynch & Fa'afo Pat (eds.), Oceanic Studies: Proceedings of the First International Conference on Oceanic Linguistics, 1-46. Pacific Linguistics C-133. Canberra: Australian National University. (ANU Open Research hdl:1885/253852; TEXT bitstream of)
sources.note: Nothing for Mondropolon: it appears only as cited forms in PAdm reconstructions (e.g. *mona 'pandanus' > Mondropolon mon; *kururV 'thunder'; *bebeke 'defecate' > pe; *kanana 'food' > kanna; *nalato 'nettle' > lanak (met.)), without stress marks. The paper's stress statements are for other languages: Wuvulu-Aua 'primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel, and.. this placement is maintained by a rule of stress shift in suffixed forms' (p.15-16) and 'Stress in Seimat generally falls on the penultimate syllable' (sec. 3.2). No Admiralties-wide prosodic generalisation is made.

sources.note: Mondropolon appears only in consonant-correspondence tables and cognate sets (e.g. *pose > pos, *lisa > nir); nothing on Mondropolon stress. General stress remarks in the book concern other languages.

sources.citation: Schooling, Stephen & Janice Schooling. 1988. A preliminary sociolinguistic and linguistic survey of Manus Province, Papua New Guinea. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 26, 211-241. Pacific Linguistics A-76. Canberra: ANU. DOI:10.15144/PL-A76.211
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'Brief grammatical notes' (pp.222-223) gives a pan-Manus phonological profile: characteristic consonants /p t k ? mb nd m n s h l r w j/ plus a prenasalised trill, no voiced/voiceless stop contrast, five vowels /i e a o u/; 'Notes on the vowels: 1. Some of the languages have length, for example Kurti and Mondropolon. 2. Some languages have voiceless vowels, for example Pak. 3. Some languages have diphthongs.' Nothing on stress, accent or tone for any language. Elsewhere: Mondropolon 54% cognate with Tulu; song books produced in Mondropolon by the Catholic mission.
